pieces.label: Section A · 第 1 篇 · 1–4 题

lines.en: M: Good morning. My name is Bob Fetterman. I'm the computer technician.
lines.zh: M：早上好。我叫鲍勃·费特曼，是电脑技术员。

lines.en: W: Didn't I call for you last week?
lines.zh: W：上周不是我打电话叫你来的吗？

lines.en: M: Maybe? I work for Alpha Maintenance. I imagine someone from your office called our central office and I'm the engineer designated to your case.
lines.zh: M：可能吧？我为 Alpha Maintenance 工作。我想应该是你们办公室有人打电话给了我们的总部，而我是负责处理你们这个问题的工程师。

lines.en: W: Yeah, I spoke to a lady there last Tuesday, which is now 10 days ago. I made it clear it was an urgent matter and please send someone as soon as possible. Couldn't you or someone else have come sooner?
lines.zh: W：是的，我上周二，也就是十天前，跟那边的一位女士谈过。我明确说过这是件急事，请尽快派人过来。你或者其他人就不能早点来吗？

lines.en: M: I'm sorry, but I'm not in charge of scheduling all logistics. I simply do not know. All I can tell you is I got the call this week and came as soon as I could.
lines.zh: M：很抱歉，但我不负责安排所有的后勤事宜。我确实不知道。我只能告诉你，我是这周接到电话的，并且已经尽可能快地赶来了。

lines.en: W: I see. Well, I'll have you know, my manager is rather indignant that it's taken you this long to come. I understand it might not be your fault, but nevertheless, you should know what the feeling is around here.
lines.zh: W：我明白了。不过我要告诉你，我的经理对你们花了这么长时间才过来相当不满。我知道这可能不是你的错，但不管怎样，你应该知道这里对此事的看法。

lines.en: M: I understand, and I'm sorry for any inconvenience. I will try to resolve your computer problem as swiftly and optimally as I can. What and where is the issue?
lines.zh: M：我明白，也很抱歉给你带来不便。我会尽我所能，尽快、妥善地解决你们的电脑问题。问题是什么，在哪里？

lines.en: W: It's this machine right here. It was running slow for a while, I guess, and gradually got worse and worse. Last Tuesday, it just stopped working altogether. If you switch it on, you will see what I mean.
lines.zh: W：就是这台机器。它运行缓慢有一阵子了，我想，然后逐渐变得越来越糟。上周二，它彻底停止工作了。你把它打开就知道我说的是什么意思了。

lines.en: M: Okay. Do you know if it's backed up?
lines.zh: M：好的。你知道它有没有备份吗？

lines.en: W: Backed up?
lines.zh: W：备份？

lines.en: M: I mean, do you know if its contents have been copied and saved somewhere else?
lines.zh: M：我的意思是，你知道里面的内容有没有被复制并保存到其他地方吗？

lines.en: W: I don't know.
lines.zh: W：我不知道。

lines.en: M: Well, depending on the ensuing operative scenario, if I need to wipe the system directories clean in order to reconfigure default protocols, then my first intervention should be to intricately retrieve all inventories that I can. Otherwise, all data that was stored on its hard drive will be forever lost.
lines.zh: M：这个嘛，具体要看接下来采取什么操作。如果我需要清空系统目录，以便重新配置默认协议，那么我的第一步应该是尽可能仔细地找回所有资料。否则，存储在硬盘上的所有数据都会永久丢失。

lines.en: W: My manager would know. Let me go get him.
lines.zh: W：我的经理应该知道。我去把他叫来。

pieces.label: Section A · 第 2 篇 · 5–8 题

lines.en: M: Have you given more thought to studying law?
lines.zh: M: 你有没有进一步考虑过学法律？

lines.en: W: I've been thinking about it a lot, yes. In fact, this is why I wished to speak to you. I wanted to hear more about what it's like.
lines.zh: W: 我确实认真考虑过很多次。事实上，这就是我想和你谈谈的原因。我想多了解一下这个职业到底是什么样的。

lines.en: M: A career in law is a beautiful thing in my opinion. Many people will say it's a boring field, but I disagree. The thing is there are many different branches of law and many different jobs.
lines.zh: M: 在我看来，从事法律工作是一件很美好的事。很多人会说这是个无聊的领域，但我不这么认为。问题在于，法律有许多不同的分支，也有许多不同的工作。

lines.en: W: You are involved with buildings and construction, right?
lines.zh: W: 你是从事建筑和施工方面工作的，对吧？

lines.en: M: Correct. I'm a solicitor, specializing in real estate. Most of my work involves mediating land disputes.
lines.zh: M: 没错。我是一名事务律师，专门从事房地产法律事务。我的大部分工作都涉及调解土地纠纷。

lines.en: W: Do you mind giving me an example?
lines.zh: W: 你介意举个例子吗？

lines.en: M: Sure. So in many cases I am employed to arbitrate between two clashing parties. Let's say for example, there are two landowners who are in a thorny disagreement about something like the borders of their adjacent plots. Someone may employ me to break the deadlock and resolve the dispute. Often my work involves negotiating agreements, plain and simple.
lines.zh: M: 当然可以。很多时候，我会受雇在两个发生冲突的当事人之间进行仲裁。比如说，有两位土地所有者，因为相邻地块的边界之类的问题而陷入棘手的争执。有人可能会聘请我来打破僵局，解决这场纠纷。很多时候，我的工作就是协商达成协议，仅此而已。

lines.en: W: So you are saying that a lot of what you do is fix people's legal issues, like you try to find a solution that benefits everyone and that prevents a problem from escalating.
lines.zh: W: 所以你的意思是，你所做的很多事情都是在解决人们的法律问题，比如努力找到一个对大家都有利的解决方案，防止问题进一步恶化。

lines.en: M: Exactly, well put. You need to remember that courts, like all bureaucracies really, can be very messy, frustrating, and expensive. For this reason, it's usually better to resolve problems outside of court whenever possible.
lines.zh: M: 没错，你说得很准确。你要记住，法院和所有官僚机构一样，往往会非常混乱、令人沮丧，而且费用高昂。因此，只要有可能，通常最好在法院之外解决问题。

lines.en: W: I see. So besides knowing the law inside out, you need good people skills, right?
lines.zh: W: 我明白了。所以除了要对法律了如指掌之外，还需要有很好的人际交往能力，对吧？

lines.en: M: Of course. Any job that involves people requires good interpersonal skills, and any law professional needs to be very eloquent at articulating that argument.
lines.zh: M: 当然。任何涉及与人打交道的工作都需要良好的人际交往能力，而任何法律从业者都需要非常善于清晰、有说服力地表达自己的观点。

lines.en: W: Right. So I've been thinking about studying criminal law. I think it sounds very interesting.
lines.zh: W: 对。所以我一直在考虑学习刑法。我觉得这听起来很有意思。

lines.en: M: Mm-hmm, yes. I'd say there's more money in property law, but the stakes are higher in criminal law. I can see how you would find it more interesting.
lines.zh: M: 嗯，是的。我想房地产法能赚更多钱，但刑法涉及的利害关系更大。我能理解你为什么会觉得它更有趣。

pieces.label: Section B · 第 1 篇 · 9–11 题

lines.en: When a person tries to access a memory, their brains quickly examine everything stored in it to find the relevant information. But as we age, many of us have difficulty retrieving memories.
lines.zh: 当一个人试图提取一段记忆时，其大脑会迅速检查其中储存的所有内容，以找出相关信息。但随着年龄增长，我们中的许多人会难以回忆起记忆。

lines.en: In a review published in the journal *Trends in Cognitive Sciences* on February 11th, researchers propose an explanation for why this might be happening: the brains of older adults allocate more space to accumulated knowledge and have more material to navigate when attempting to access memories. While this wealth of prior knowledge can make memory retrieval challenging, the researchers say it has its upsides—this life experience can aid with creativity and decision-making.
lines.zh: 研究人员在2月11日发表于《认知科学趋势》杂志的一篇综述中提出了这一现象可能发生的原因：老年人的大脑会为积累的知识分配更多空间，因此在尝试提取记忆时需要在更多内容中进行搜索。研究人员表示，尽管这些丰富的既有知识会使记忆提取变得更具挑战性，但它也有积极的一面——这些人生经历能够帮助人们进行创造和决策。

lines.en: Researchers Tarek Amer, Jordana Wynn and Lynn Hasher looked at several behavioral and brain imaging studies, which show that older adults have difficulty suppressing information that is no longer relevant and that when searching for a specific memory, they often retrieve other, irrelevant memories along with it. The studies also showed that when given a cognitive task, older adults rely more heavily on previous knowledge than younger adults do.
lines.zh: 研究人员塔雷克·阿梅尔、乔丹娜·温和林恩·哈舍尔考察了多项行为研究和脑成像研究。这些研究显示，老年人难以抑制已经不再相关的信息；在寻找某一特定记忆时，他们常常会连同其他无关记忆一起提取出来。研究还显示，在面对认知任务时，老年人比年轻人更加依赖既有知识。

lines.en: While the researchers focus primarily on the difficulties that these disorderly, crowded memories may pose, they also highlight a few situations in which these same memory patterns may be useful. "Evidence suggests that older adults show preserved, and at times enhanced, creativity as a function of enriched memories," the researchers write. They further hypothesize that older adults may be well served by their prior knowledge when it comes to decision-making, where they can pull on their accumulated wisdom.
lines.zh: 尽管研究人员主要关注这些杂乱、拥挤的记忆可能造成的困难，但他们也指出了几种相同记忆模式可能发挥作用的情形。研究人员写道：“证据表明，老年人的创造力得益于记忆内容的丰富，不仅得以保持，有时还会有所增强。”他们进一步推测，在进行决策时，老年人可能会受益于自己的既有知识，因为他们能够运用积累的智慧。

pieces.label: Section B · 第 2 篇 · 12–15 题

lines.en: There are at least four major problems with work in America today.
lines.zh: 如今，美国的工作至少存在四个主要问题。

lines.en: First, work can be alienating. Workers are often not in control of how they work, when they work, what is done with the goods and services they produce, and what is done with the profits made from their work.
lines.zh: 首先，工作可能导致异化。劳动者往往无法掌控自己的工作方式、工作时间、对其生产的商品和服务的处置方式，以及对其劳动所创造利润的处置方式。

lines.en: Second, workers are not paid the full value of their labor. Real wages have not kept pace with productivity, driving economic inequality and a decline in labor's share of income.
lines.zh: 其次，劳动者没有获得其劳动的全部价值。实际工资未能与生产率同步增长，导致经济不平等加剧，并使劳动收入在总收入中的占比下降。

lines.en: Third, people are time poor. In the U.S., full time employees work an average of 8.72 hours per day despite productivity increases. Long working hours contribute to the feeling of "time poverty", which has an adverse effect on psychological well-being.
lines.zh: 第三，人们缺乏时间。尽管生产率有所提高，美国的全职雇员每天平均工作8.72小时。长时间工作加剧了“时间贫困”感，并对心理健康产生不利影响。

lines.en: Fourth, automation puts jobs and wages at risk. Technological innovation could in theory liberate people from the 40-hour work week. But unless changes are made to the structure of work, automation will simply exert downward pressure on wages and further diminish work opportunities.
lines.zh: 第四，自动化使工作岗位和工资面临风险。从理论上说，技术创新可以使人们摆脱每周40小时的工作制。但是，除非对工作结构进行改变，否则自动化只会给工资施加下行压力，并进一步减少工作机会。

lines.en: So, what can be done to alleviate these problems? There are competing visions of the best way to arrive at a solution. One vision is what's known as the "post-work" position. The post-work theorists believe that work should not hold a central position in our lives or take up so much of our time. They assert that although doing some work might be necessary, meaning, purpose and social value reside in the communities and relationships built and sustained outside of the workplace. Thus, life should be seen as an end in itself.
lines.zh: 那么，可以采取什么措施来缓解这些问题呢？对于如何实现解决方案，人们存在相互竞争的构想。其中一种构想被称为“后工作”立场。后工作理论家认为，工作不应在我们的生活中占据核心地位，也不应占用我们如此多的时间。他们主张，尽管从事一定的工作可能是必要的，但意义、目标和社会价值存在于工作场所以外建立并维系的社区和关系之中。因此，生活本身应被视为目的。

pieces.label: Section C · 第 1 篇 · 16–18 题

lines.en: Recent studies show that self-control and persistence increase academic outcomes, independence of IQ. Even our personal beliefs about efforts can affect academic outcomes. Children who think effort leads to achievement outperform those who believe ability is a fixed trait. Given the link between persistence and academic success, decisions about efforts are particularly important in childhood.
lines.zh: 近期研究表明，自我控制和坚持不懈能够提升学业表现，而这一作用独立于智商。甚至我们对努力的个人看法也会影响学业表现。认为努力能够带来成就的儿童，比那些认为能力是一种固定特质的儿童表现更好。鉴于坚持不懈与学业成功之间的联系，童年时期对是否付出努力的判断尤为重要。

lines.en: Yet, relatively little research has explored how young children learn what's worth the effort. We all know that infants are keen observers of the social world, but they're not just idly watching; they are tiny learning machines. They can generalize such abstract concepts as causal relationships and social roles from just a few examples. Even a 15-month-old infant can outperform a high level computer in such tasks. Could infants also make broad generalizable inferences from a few examples when it comes to effort? If so, then maybe persistence isn't simply a character trait. Maybe it's flexible and adaptable based on social context.
lines.zh: 然而，相对而言，很少有研究探讨幼儿是如何学会判断什么值得付出努力的。我们都知道，婴儿善于观察社会世界，但他们并非只是无所事事地观看；他们是微型的学习机器。他们仅凭几个例子，就能概括出因果关系和社会角色等抽象概念。即使是15个月大的婴儿，在这类任务中的表现也可能超过高水平的计算机。当涉及努力时，婴儿是否也能根据少数几个例子作出广泛且可推广的推断？如果可以，那么坚持不懈也许并不只是某种性格特征，而是会根据社会情境灵活调整、适应变化的能力。

lines.en: To explore this question, we showed 15-month-old babies one of two things—an experimenter working hard to achieve two different goals, or an experimenter who effortlessly reached each goal. Then we introduced the baby to a novel music toy that seemed as if it could be activated by pushing a big button on top. The button could be pressed down, but didn't actually activate anything. Out of sight of the babies, we turned on the music toy with a hidden button so that they heard the toy making music. We gave the babies the music toy and left the room. Then analysts who didn't know which condition each baby was in, watched video tapes of the experiment and counted how many times babies tried to activate the toy by pressing the button.
lines.zh: 为了探究这一问题，我们向15个月大的婴儿展示两种情形中的一种：一名实验者努力工作以实现两个不同的目标，或者一名毫不费力地实现每个目标的实验者。随后，我们向婴儿介绍一个新颖的音乐玩具，看起来似乎可以通过按下顶部的大按钮来启动。这个按钮可以被按下，但实际上并不会启动任何功能。在婴儿看不见的地方，我们用一个隐藏按钮打开了音乐玩具，让他们听到玩具发出音乐。我们把音乐玩具交给婴儿，然后离开房间。之后，不知道每个婴儿属于哪种实验条件的分析人员观看了实验录像，并统计婴儿试图通过按下按钮启动玩具的次数。

lines.en: Across one study and a pre-registered duplication, babies who had seen an adult persist and succeed push the button about twice as many times as those who saw an adult effortlessly succeed. In other words, babies learned that effort was valuable after watching just two examples of an adult working hard and succeeding. Part of what's exciting about this finding is that the babies didn't just imitate the adult's actions. Instead, they generalized the value of effort to a novel task. The experimenter never demonstrated pushing a button or trying to make music. Instead, the babies learned from different examples of effortful actions that the new toy probably also required persistence.
lines.zh: 在一项研究及其预注册重复实验中，看过成年人坚持不懈并取得成功的婴儿，按下按钮的次数约为看过成年人毫不费力地取得成功的婴儿的两倍。换言之，婴儿仅仅观察成年人努力工作并取得成功的两个例子后，就学会了努力是有价值的。这一发现令人兴奋的部分原因在于，婴儿并不只是模仿成年人的动作。相反，他们把努力的价值推广到了一个全新的任务中。实验者从未示范按按钮或尝试让玩具播放音乐。相反，婴儿从不同的努力行为示例中学到，这个新玩具可能也需要坚持不懈。

pieces.label: Section C · 第 2 篇 · 19–21 题

lines.en: If chronic lateness has taken over your life and turned into a defining trait of who you are, it's likely that you're losing out on job offers, recreational opportunities, friendships, and more. If you are showing up late to your own life, get organized, prioritize punctuality, and address any underlying causes.
lines.zh: 如果长期迟到已经占据了你的生活，并变成了定义你这个人的特征，那么你很可能正因此错失工作机会、休闲活动、友谊以及更多其他东西。如果你在自己的人生中都迟到，请做好组织安排，优先重视守时，并处理任何潜在原因。

lines.en: When you have to be somewhere, try to arrive 15 to 30 minutes before you need to. If you always run late, that means you must be failing to account for something you always do. Anticipate that by giving yourself extra time to arrive. Keep track of whether or not you actually do arrive early. You might find that leaving early gets you to places exactly on time.
lines.zh: 当你必须前往某个地方时，尽量提前15到30分钟到达。如果你总是迟到，这意味着你一定没有考虑到某件自己总会做的事情。通过给自己预留额外时间来提前应对这一点。记录自己是否真的提前到达。你可能会发现，提前出发反而能让你恰好准时到达目的地。

lines.en: Set two alarms. Set one alarm that lets you know it's time to drop what you're doing and a second alarm that means you need to walk out the door. Obey the alarms. As soon as the first alarm goes off, stop what you're doing. If it's something you'll be coming back to, like a project for work, make a note to remind yourself where you left off. Grab everything you need and make sure you know how to get where you're going. Aim to be out the door and on your way before the second alarm rings. This will only work if you take the alarms seriously, so make sure you react as soon as you hear them.
lines.zh: 设置两个闹钟。设置一个闹钟，提醒你该放下手头正在做的事情；再设置第二个闹钟，表示你必须出门了。遵守闹钟的提醒。第一个闹钟一响，就停止手头的事情。如果那是你之后还会继续做的事情，比如工作项目，就记下来提醒自己做到哪里。拿上所有需要的东西，并确保自己知道如何到达目的地。目标是在第二个闹钟响起之前出门上路。只有认真对待这两个闹钟，这种方法才会奏效，所以一听到闹钟响就要立即作出反应。

lines.en: Prepare for the day ahead. Have all of your notes and materials organized well in advance of each event, so that all you have to do is grab them and go when it's the actual day. If mornings are a struggle for you, do as much as you can to ready yourself the night before. Before you go to bed, lay out your clothes and pack your bag for the next day.
lines.zh: 为第二天做好准备。提前整理好每项活动所需的全部笔记和材料，这样到了当天，你只需拿上它们就可以出发。如果早晨对你来说很难熬，就尽可能在前一晚做好准备。睡觉前，准备好第二天要穿的衣服，并收拾好包。

lines.en: Learn to leave time in between tasks and meetings. It soon becomes unbearable to shift between one meeting and another without space in between. If you overschedule yourself, however, you'll arrive late as soon as you hit a bump. As well as giving you space, this time also acts as a buffer between events, which can be borrowed from, should you be held up in a prior meeting, allowing you to still get to the next one on time. Calculate transit time between activities and then add 10 to 30 minutes for unexpected delays.
lines.zh: 学会在任务和会议之间留出时间。在两个会议之间没有任何间隔地转换，很快就会让人难以忍受。然而，如果你的日程安排得过于紧凑，一遇到意外情况，你就会迟到。除了为你提供喘息空间外，这段时间还可以充当活动之间的缓冲；如果你在前一个会议上被耽搁了，就可以借用这段时间，从而仍能准时参加下一个会议。计算各项活动之间的交通时间，然后再增加10到30分钟，以应对意外延误。

pieces.label: Section C · 第 3 篇 · 22–25 题

lines.en: Do you think Bostonians put out the welcome mat? Do you find other cities to be more or less polite? Different cities have different feels for visitors. Some are friendly and open; some are formal and distant. Boston tends to seem hurried and sometimes a little rude. That's what some tourists have said. One study found that people here are less willing to volunteer to help strangers than those residents of other U.S. cities. Take a close look next time you're in Boston, and here are some of the things you'll probably see: people smoking in the subway stations despite the frequent reminders not to do so; pedestrians walking when the crosswalk lights say not to do so, ignoring the cars; car drivers speeding, making a loud noise with the horn and occasionally cursing at each other. Drivers who can't be bothered to find a place to park, but instead simply turn on their blinker and stop in the middle of the street.
lines.zh: 你认为波士顿人会铺上迎宾垫吗？你觉得其他城市的人更有礼貌，还是不那么有礼貌？不同的城市给游客的感觉各不相同。有些城市友好而开放，有些则拘谨而疏远。波士顿往往给人一种行色匆匆、有时还有些粗鲁的感觉。一些游客就是这么说的。一项研究发现，这里的人主动自愿帮助陌生人的意愿低于美国其他城市的居民。下次你在波士顿时，不妨仔细看看，你很可能会看到以下一些情景：尽管地铁站经常提醒人们不要吸烟，还是有人在那里吸烟；人行横道信号灯显示禁止通行时，行人仍然无视汽车继续行走；汽车司机超速行驶，大声按喇叭，偶尔还互相破口大骂。有些司机懒得找停车位，反而只是打开转向灯，把车停在马路中央。

lines.en: Sometimes Bostonians seem like they're just too busy to be polite. Why is their city like that? Former U.S. representative Chester Atkins says it's because the Puritan founding fathers were themselves impatient and bad-tempered, and had little time for courtesy. That culture has carried down to the present day, he believes. Boston College professor Thomas O'Connor thinks a contributing factor is Boston's history as a city where each new group of immigrants was treated with suspicion and exclusion. That's given Boston a sense of clannishness and reserve, he thinks. The idea of a stranger greeting another stranger is simply not part of the local culture, he says. People will begin a conversation with someone they know, but not with a stranger. Ralph Whitehead, a professor of journalism at the University of Massachusetts at Amherst, thinks it's because Boston's upper class used manners to make class distinctions. By being snobbish about manners, Proper Bostonians made other people scornful of courtesy, he says.
lines.zh: 有时波士顿人给人的感觉是，他们只是太忙了，顾不上讲礼貌。他们的城市为什么会这样？美国前众议员切斯特·阿特金斯说，这是因为那些清教徒开拓者本身就缺乏耐心、脾气暴躁，没有多少时间讲究礼节。他认为，这种文化一直延续到了今天。波士顿学院教授托马斯·奥康纳认为，另一个促成因素是波士顿的历史：每一批新来的移民都曾受到猜疑和排斥。他认为，这使波士顿形成了一种排外和矜持的气质。他说，陌生人主动向另一个陌生人打招呼，根本不属于当地文化的一部分。人们会与自己认识的人开始交谈，却不会与陌生人交谈。马萨诸塞大学阿默斯特分校新闻学教授拉尔夫·怀特黑德认为，这是因为波士顿上流社会曾利用礼仪来划分阶层。他说，波士顿那些讲究“正统礼仪”的人对礼仪表现得势利，从而使其他人开始鄙视礼节。

lines.en: Some say that's just the way Boston is and that the city will never change. Still, other cities with reputations for worse rudeness are trying hard to change their images. Paris is one example where people are trying to be friendly. New York City is another. There, the city is trying to persuade subway riders to be more considerate. If those cities can make the effort, maybe Boston should as well.
lines.zh: 有人说，波士顿就是这样，这座城市永远不会改变。不过，一些因粗鲁而声名更差的城市正在努力改变自己的形象。巴黎就是一个例子，那里的人们正在努力变得友好。纽约市是另一个例子。在那里，市政府正试图劝说地铁乘客更加体谅他人。如果那些城市都能付出努力，波士顿或许也应该这样做。
